To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we provide an algorithm to find the optimal bound over counterfactual queries in a causal diagram, and we provide a reduction that maps the original, general SCM to a dual, well-behaved SCM, where exogenous variables are all discrete.

(i) all counterfactual queries in a causal model can be bounded by a special family (called the dual family) of structural causal models, where the exogenous (unobserved) variables are discrete; (ii) the problem of bounding a counterfactual query in a causal model reduces to a convex optimization program over the parameters of an SCM in the dual family; and (iii) Monte Carlo algorithms can be used to approximate the optimal bounds from a sample of observational data.

(1) we provide a new method to bound counterfactuals in a general setting; (2) the method relies on a new reduction to a more well-behavied space where unobserved variables take values in a discrete, finite domain; (3) the method is computationally tractable and validated on synthetic datasets.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (i) What are the bounds of the counterfactual distributions over finite observed variables in an arbitrary causal model, and how do we find the best bounds? (ii) What are the implications of these bounds on causal inference?
a fundamental problem in causal inference: how to identify bounds on counterfactuals in a given causal diagram.
a general problem: how to bound the distribution of counterfactuals from observational data, and qualitative causal assumptions, in the form of causal diagrams.

the problem of bounding the counterfactual distributions in a causal diagram is a finite-dimensional, convex optimization problem, and hence is computationally tractable.
